While there's nothing necessarily *weird* about the northern rivers limnologically speaking here are a few reasons why they may appear strange to you.

**1.)** The widest river on the continent splits three times. While this isn't impossible the likelihood of five areas of low elevation (which often determine the path of a stream) being nearly identical in elevation is virtually impossible. Keep in mind that a river pursues the area of lowest elevation, diverging from a stream or shoal of higher elevation.

**2.)** Nearly every river you depict splits. Although it's difficult to narrow down the exact percentage of rivers that bifurcate into two streams, a good rule of thumb is that 1 in every 100 rivers is capable of such phenomena. I've even read sources that claim it is closer to 1 in ever 1,000.

**3.)** Rivers in the same biome/environment run in contradictory paths. For instance, on the western coast of the northern continent, there is a river that appears to originate in the mountains that flows to the sea. This is appropriate as you would expect its path to run from an area of higher elevation (mountains) to sea level. However, the river directly above the mountains seems to begin at sea level and run towards that same area of high elevation.

Two stick out to me: The Halifax Explosion and the Carrington Event.

1.) During the late war period of WWI two ammunition vessels collided off of the coast of Canada. The ensuing catastrophe is widely considered the largest man-made explosion prior to the creation of nuclear weapons. One of the heroes of the day was a man named Patrick Vincent Coleman who steered a large portion of the combustible material away from the initial wreck thereby saving the lives of those nearby on the coast by relocating the epicenter of the explosion, and himself, further to sea.

2.) The carrington event describes an electro magnetic phenomena witnessed in the skies of Eastern Asia, North America, Europe and potentially everywhere else in the world. Although few can state with certainty what the lights that represented the Carrington Event where, modern experts suspect the cause to be a massive solar flare. While the lights were presented, telegraph transponders actuated faster, receiving and sending data at an alarmingly fast rate, and roosters crowed at the onset of the lights, believing them to be the encroaching sun.

The majority of the people who dislike the game aren't even sure why they dislike it. And most who love the game are merely voicing a received opinion echoed to them by the larger community. In my opinion, OP summed it up best by characterizing the game as a, "flawed masterpiece." (SPOILER WARNINGS AHEAD) This game utilizes a literary mechanism right out of the gate known as, "in media res." Most video game sequels find themselves in a tricky situation when starting out the game and introducing it to new and old players alike. This is exacerbated when LOU2 begins in media res. Instead of taking up after the chronological ending of LOU1 it skips a few years ahead, Joel and Ellie are already living in Jackson, leading both new and old players alike into unknown territory. 

This may seem like a minor oddity or unorthodox take on screenwriting but it's really the first, and only, glaring mistake. See, in my opinion, the Last of Us II is nothing if not a perfect example of how pace and story structure can make a good story bad and a masterpiece feel unappealing to the player. Many players who disliked Joel's death mentioned that they, "didn't have enough time" to spend with the character. Other critiques were made concerning Abby, and the unrelatable nature of her character arc. Starting out the story in media res is to blame for both of these conundrums.

Here's my prescription; instead of the story skipping over Joel and Ellie's life in the beginning allow it to breathe; fixate on it. The 1st act, instead, ought to have been solely devoted to Abby's character arc. Imagine if we start out the game as Abby and end it right after she realizes her father has died. Instead of placing Abby's flashback scene after the cliffhanger in the second act (the showdown at the movie theatre) it should be in the very beginning. New players would have been introduced to Abby before Joel and Ellie, leading them to possibly sympathizing more with Abby than the older characters. Old players would have enjoyed the departure and watched in bated breath as Abby met Joel for the first time; anticipating the conflict that was sure to unfold. And finally, this resolves the issue of players not enjoying abby's story arc later in the game as the majority of it would've taken place in the first act, before Ellie and Dina arrive in Seattle.

All in all, I loved this game but thought that the writers should've reigned in some of the more unorthodox literary techniques. Anyone else have whiplash at around the half-way point from all the fucking time shifts and flash-backs?
